Faye Dunaway was a revelation in Network. Mommie Dearest almost ruined her career, but it’s beloved as a cult favorite. You see her and well I just give her the benefit of the doubt and pull for her. To come back from a ruined career to do Barfly… just wow. She asked the director on Mommie Dearest to tell her if she was going too far. 

Melissa McCarthy. To go from Mike and Molly to Bridesmaids was a hat trick. Then going from comedy to do Can You Ever Forgive Me. I’ve never been so impressed by such a feat displaying so much talent. I’d watch her in a commercial for shoes for cats.

People identify with vulnerability. No one says "I'm only human" after they break a world record. It's why Ripley's character in Alien is still the archetype of the modern hero. You see her scared and at risk in the first half of the movie, so her brave determination at the end rings true. It's an act of defiance. If she was like that throughout the whole movie you'd think she was arrogant and never in any real danger. I'm convinced people who write "brave" characters that never show weakness have never done anything courageous in their entire life.

> Question, What makes an actor endearing?

An acting coach once told me this: What we consider a good actor has very little to do with skill, talent, or the work they've put into the craft. Don't get me wrong, those things do matter and they can transform a good actor into a great actor, but what truly makes an actor endearing, compelling, and someone we want to watch is one thing: do we like their face?

That's it. Do we like their face? Now, this could mean someone is attractive and general audiences like looking at them for that reason. But it doesn't exclusively mean attraction. Some people just have a face that you enjoy looking at. You enjoy how it moves and the shapes it makes when expressing different emotions. You like the way they can vibrate their vocal chords to produce sounds you enjoy. 

Having an interesting face is a key step to becoming an actor.

This is a complicated answer.

Heroic type actors like James Stewart or Tom Hanks are generally very charming right from the gate.  

The ability to play characters that are in the emotional wringer makes it easy to empathize with a lot of these individuals (the scene in which Jim Lovell is imagining himself on the moon is quietly devastating)

But then again, I think on the flipside..

I think there are actors who bring charm to villainous characters.

The lazy example would be Tom Hiddleston as Loki.

Behind the sinister face is a likable gaze of rich gem like eyes.

For more classical examples, Vincent Price and his regal demeanor, and Boris Karloff with a pitiful charm in the early 30s Frankenstein. 

Maybe the element of genuine terror for Anthony Hopkins in
' silence of the lambs._

And so I think the answer is for audiences to both appreciate the charisma and effectiveness of actors while at the same time kind of seeing a faint image of themselves through performance.

It's about particular facial gestures that make visible a certain sort of character. Any character can be made likable by cutting the shot at the right moment so as to segment the facial expression correctly for recognition as that sort of character; plus good lighting. Most people don't express much individual character at all, so when someone consistently exudes a lot of it, this makes it easier to capture or even almost foolproof to capture if they are also good at starting and stopping their facial gestures at opportune moments for the camera. I suspect these actors that are highly watchable for you, that what you like is seeing a glimpse of the actor's character in the story character (because the character is already fully expressed), not a glimpse of the character in the body (when the actor is still struggling to express any character at all).

This is what I would say about Paul Giamatti. I like seeing him in all his roles, and can’t wait for The Holdovers. He also gives the impression that he puts a bit of himself in every role, which would show vulnerability, a trait some else already mentioned.

That there are acting coaches out there telling actors this is disturbing. 

First, because you can’t really control whether you have an “interesting” face. I mean, you can get plastic surgery or something like that, but that’s probably gonna make your face less expressive. And you still wouldn’t know whether the changes have made your face more “interesting”. 

Second, this fixation with the face is a great way to kill your acting. If you’re putting all your focus on one part of your body, you’re going to become very self conscious, you’re going to lock yourself up with tension, and you’re going to deaden the rest of your body. The actors with the most expressiveness in their faces are the ones that are engaging their whole apparatus. We can see a lot coming from their faces because their whole body is alive. 

Third, it’s just such a shallow way of looking at acting. The problem with so many questions about acting like OP’s is that they confuse the actor for the acting. An actor can be likable, endearing, attractive or whatever, but that doesn’t mean their acting is good or even great. Really when we talk about acting, we shouldn’t be talking solely about the individual actor. We should be talking how well they uplift the scene or the movie. 

Something I notice that’s said about great dancers is that they’re great partners. They bring out more in who they’re working with. This is something completely missing in discussions about acting. It’s actually seen as a compliment to say that the actor “blew everyone away” in a scene. Like why should that be something to be praised?

I could just rant all day about this stuff. The whole culture around acting is awful and it’s why acting rarely reaches great levels.

Rick Moranis in Little Shop of Horrors was so endearing that they pretty much entirely changed the character from the stageplay to be a likable underdog instead of a creep. His influence in the performance was so great that test audiences hated seeing the original ending, so they made a happier one.

I think it's an understand of the lower/middle class that makes many actors endearing, and a lot of modern actors simply lack that. Harry Dean Stanton, Moranis, Fonda, theres a shared sympathy for the average joe that these three, for example, all share that exudes through their performances.

That's why it's "Do we like their face" and not "are we attracted to their face." Devil is in those details.

I think it varies from actor to actor, and often the specific roles too. 

Sometimes it's just generally obvious. Like John Candy absolutely radiated warmth and charisma all the time. It was simply a joy to watch him whenever he was on screen. 

Sometimes it's the creativity or effort they put in coming through. I got this from both Johnny Depp and Geoffrey Rush in Pirates of the Caribbean, and Kristen Wiig in Knocked Up. You could tell how much fun they were having playing those characters. 

Some people are just incredibly beautiful, and that can be fun to watch on it's own. 

Then there's the inexplicable ones. People like Pete Davidson. He's just an average looking guy, probably leaning towards odd looking really. He's not a remarkably talented actor, and he doesn't really exude effort either. But he's got something about him that's slightly magnetic. "The X Factor" or whatever you want to call it. He's fun to watch in an indefinable way.

Just started watching Barry, on season 4. Bill Harder isn’t necessarily some esteemed actor, but his face is extremely distinct and he has great expressions. He’s not an intimidating guy by any means, but when he’s exhibiting rage? He’s pretty damn terrifying. It’s all in the eyes, the snarl. He’s amazing in the show. 

What you said also reminds me of Godfather 2. Al Pacino barely has any dialogue in the film, yet he communicates perfectly with his eyes and expressions.

I think Philip Seymour Hoffman was the best actor of his generation and part of that was I just loved watching him and looking at his face. The way it emoted and contorted was fascinating and never not compelling. But equally as compelling to me was the way he spoke. The emphasis he put on certain words and the mannerisms he used throughout his whole body. He always became someone new.

Jack Nicholson mentioned at one point he was starting to forget lines on his last movie. I think he'd rather retain his solid career of movies and live a quiet retirement out of the public eye then go out like Bruce Willis in below-par movies to cater to the memory issues in old age.

With Welles though you have to sort of take him in any interview in the context that Hollywood fucked with pretty much every movie he made after Citizen Kane. A real bummer what happened to his career. Orson Welles original version of The Magnificent Ambersons is one of the lost great films.

Wow! Great question!

I’d say, aside from choosing roles that make the character the protagonist, the most endearing quality for me is reaction. Actors that are two dimensional can be endearing, but I think a lot of them also happen to be comedy actors prone to being more animated and expressive.

The first actor that came to mind here, for me, is Sam Rockwell. I think he does a good job being present in his scenes, but also during the more quiet moments. There’s a sort of vulnerability in his expressions that feel like they can be broken at any moment by whoever is adjacent to him on screen. He has an almost underdog charisma that, rather than detract from the other actors on screen, quietly enhances them. He’s never waiting to say his lines. He’s present; and his presence seems to enhance every scene he’s in because it makes everyone else more present. I dunno. I think that “thing” is less about good looks and more about making everyone around you better, by being THAT good. 

A lot of actors can carry their weight in solo performances, or by being attractive and charismatic; while others are simply REALLY GOOD at being on set, and you can SEE how good they make everyone around them by being good at what they do.

In “The Story Solution”, Eric Edson has a theory about likability of fictional characters which I think apples to real life people as well. He lists nine essential attributes for likable characters:

-Courage
- Has some kind of Unfair Injury
-Skill
-Funny
-Just Plain Nice
-In Danger
-Loved By Friends And Family
-Hard Working
-Obsessed

In order for character to be likable, they only need to have at least five out of nine. Many people
have more, but five is the minimum. In my assessment, Orson Welles checks 6 of the 9.
